title: Do People Need Feedback?
author: Nick Hart
summary: Drawing on Buckingham and Goodall's 'Nine Lies About Work,' Nick Hart challenges school leaders to rethink feedback as a management tool. The central finding is that people don't primarily need feedback—they need attention, and specifically positive attention directed at what they do best. Research shows that employees receiving predominantly positive attention to their strengths show the highest engagement and productivity. Hart distinguishes between 'mistakes fixing' (a tool to prevent failure) and genuine attention to moments of excellence (a tool to build performance)—arguing these are categorically different objectives that school leaders routinely conflate. Powerful recognition involves not just telling someone they performed well, but describing what the observer actually experienced when the moment of excellence caught their attention. For school leaders, this means deliberately carving out time to notice and articulate what colleagues do well. The Pygmalion effect—where teachers' expectations of students shape outcomes—may extend to leaders: the attention and expectations leaders communicate to teachers could shape teacher performance in similar ways. Effective positive attention requires genuine expertise, however; you can only authentically describe what you saw if you know what excellent teaching looks like.
points: * People need attention, not feedback—specifically positive attention to what they do best drives the highest engagement and productivity, according to Buckingham and Goodall's organizational research. * Powerful recognition goes beyond 'well done': leaders should describe what they experienced when a moment of excellence caught their attention, making the response genuinely personal and specific rather than generic. * 'Mistakes fixing' is a tool to prevent failure; positive attention to excellence is a tool to build performance—these are categorically different objectives that school leaders often conflate under the heading of 'feedback.' * The Pygmalion effect (teachers' expectations of students shape student outcomes) may extend upward: the attention and expectations leaders direct at teachers may similarly shape teacher performance. * Effective positive attention requires genuine expertise—to authentically describe what you saw in a colleague's practice, you must have deep knowledge of excellent teaching and learning.
quotes: If you want improvement, then your highest priority interrupt should be whenever someone on your team does something that really works. The goal is to consciously spend your days alert to those times when someone on your team does something so easily and effectively that it rocks you, just a little, and then to find a way of telling that person what you just saw.
The authors say that it is not feedback that people need, it is attention and when this is combined with psychological safety, people work hard and stay.

They describe a subtle twist on praise that involves not just telling the person how well they performed, but describing what you experienced when the moment of excellence caught your attention. They say that nothing is more genuine nor powerful than explaining what it made you think or realise.
The authors make an interesting point on dealing with people's mistakes - mistakes fixing is a tool to prevent failure rather than a tool to create excellent performance.
What is always true is our reaction to what we see, as the authors suggest, and it is the power of this attention that might be worth harnessing.
